statement: Given two spheres about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.
heath_proof: Let two spheres be conceived about the same centre A; thus it is required to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface. Let the spheres be cut by any plane through the centre; then the sections will be circles, inasmuch as the sphere was produced by the diameter remaining fixed and the semicircle being carried round it; [XI. Def. 14] hence, in whatever position we conceive the semicircle to be, the plane carried through it will produce a circle on the circumference of the sphere. And it is manifest that this circle is the greatest possible, inasmuch as the diameter of the sphere, which is of course the diameter both of the semicircle and of the circle, is greater than all the straight lines drawn across in the circle or the sphere. Let then BCDE be the circle in the greater sphere, and FGH the circle in the lesser sphere; let two diameters in them, BD, CE, be drawn at right angles to one another; then, given the two circles BCDE, FGH about the same centre, let there be inscribed in the greater circle BCDE an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle FGH, let BK, KL, LM   ME be its sides in the quadrant BE. let KA be joined and carried through to N, let AO be set up from the point A at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE, and let it meet the surface of the sphere at O, and through AO and each of the straight lines BD, KN let planes be carried; they will then make greatest circles on the surface of the sphere, for the reason stated. Let them make such, and in them let BOD, KON be the semicircles on BD, KN. Now, since OA is at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE, therefore all the planes through OA are also at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE; [XI. 18] hence the semicircles BOD, KON are also at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE. And, since the semicircles BED, BOD, KON are equal, for they are on the equal diameters BD, KN, therefore the quadrants BE, BO, KO are also equal to one another. Therefore there are as many straight lines in the quadrants BO, KO equal to the straight lines BK, KL, LM, ME as there are sides of the polygon in the quadrant BE. Let them be inscribed, and let them be BP, PQ, QR, RO and KS, ST, TU, UO, let SP, TQ, UR be joined, and from P, S let perpendiculars be drawn to the plane of the circle BCDE; [XI. 11] these will fall on BD, KN, the common sections of the planes, inasmuch as the planes of BOD, KON are also at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE. [cf. XI. Def. 4] Let them so fall, and let them be PV, SW, and let WV be joined. Now since, in the equal semicircles BOD, KON, equal straight lines BP, KS have been cut off, and the perpendiculars PV, SW have been drawn, therefore PV is equal to SW, and BV to KW. [III. 27, I. 26] But the whole BA is also equal to the whole KA; therefore the remainder VA is also equal to the remainder WA; therefore, as BV is to VA, so is KW to WA; therefore WV is parallel to KB. [VI. 2] And, since each of the straight lines PV, SW is at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE, therefore PV is parallel to SW. [XI. 6] But it was also proved equal to it; therefore WV, SP are also equal and parallel. [I. 33] And, since WV is parallel to SP, while WV is parallel to KB, therefore SP is also parallel to KB. [XI. 9] And BP, KS join their extremities; therefore the quadrilateral KBPS is in one plane, inasmuch as, if two straight lines be parallel, and points be taken at random on each of them, the straight line joining the points is in the same plane with the parallels. [XI. 7] For the same reason each of the quadrilaterals SPQT, TQRU is also in one plane. But the triangle URO is also in one plane. [XI. 2] If then we conceive straight lines joined from the points P, S, Q, T, R, U to A, there will be constructed a certain polyhedral solid figure between the circumferences BO, KO, consisting of pyramids of which the quadrilaterals KBPS, SPQT, TQRU and the triangle URO are the bases and the point A the vertex. And, if we make the same construction in the case of each of the sides KL, LM, ME as in the case of BK, and further in the case of the remaining three quadrants, there will be constructed a certain polyhedral figure inscribed in the sphere and contained by pyramids, of which the said quadrilaterals and the triangle URO, and the others corresponding to them, are the bases and the point A the vertex. I say that the said polyhedron will not touch the lesser sphere at the surface on which the circle FGH is. Let AX be drawn from the point A perpendicular to the plane of the quadrilateral KBPS, and let it meet the plane at the point X; [XI. 11] let XB, XK be joined. Then, since AX is at right angles to the plane of the quadrilateral KBPS, therefore it is also at right angles to all the straight lines which meet it and are in the plane of the quadrilateral. [XI. Def. 3] Therefore AX is at right angles to each of the straight lines BX, XK. And, since AB is equal to AK, the square on AB is also equal to the square on AK. And the squares on AX, XB are equal to the square on AB, for the angle at X is right; [I. 47] and the squares on AX, XK are equal to the square on AK. [id.] Therefore the squares on AX, XB are equal to the squares on AX, XK. Let the square on AX be subtracted from each; therefore the remainder, the square on BX, is equal to the remainder, the square on XK; therefore BX is equal to XK. Similarly we can prove that the straight lines joined from X to P, S are equal to each of the straight lines BX, XK. Therefore the circle described with centre X and distance one of the straight lines XB, XK will pass through P, S also, and KBPS will be a quadrilateral in a circle. Now, since KB is greater than WV, while WV is equal to SP, therefore KB is greater than SP. But KB is equal to each of the straight lines KS, BP; therefore each of the straight lines KS, BP is greater than SP. And, since KBPS is a quadrilateral in a circle, and KB, BP, KS are equal, and PS less, and BX is the radius of the circle, therefore the square on KB is greater than double of the square on BX. Let KZ be drawn from K perpendicular to BV. Then, since BD is less than double of DZ, and, as BD is to DZ, so is the rectangle DB, BZ to the rectangle DZ, ZB, if a square be described upon BZ and the parallelogram on ZD be completed, then the rectangle DB, BZ is also less than double of the rectangle DZ, ZB. And, if KD be joined, the rectangle DB, BZ is equal to the square on BK, and the rectangle DZ, ZB equal to the square on KZ; [III. 31, VI. 8 and Por.] therefore the square on KB is less than double of the square on KZ. But the square on KB is greater than double of the square on BX; therefore the square on KZ is greater than the square on BX. And, since BA is equal to KA, the square on BA is equal to the square on AK. And the squares on BX, XA are equal to the square on BA, and the squares on KZ, ZA equal to the square on KA; [I. 47] therefore the squares on BX, XA are equal to the squares on KZ, ZA, and of these the square on KZ is greater than the square on BX; therefore the remainder, the square on ZA, is less than the square on XA. Therefore AX is greater than AZ; therefore AX is much greater than AG. And AX is the perpendicular on one base of the polyhedron, and AG on the surface of the lesser sphere; hence the polyhedron will not touch the lesser sphere on its surface. Therefore, given two spheres about the same centre, a polyhedral solid has been inscribed in the greater sphere which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.
ai_proof_text:
12.17
**Statement:** Given two spheres about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.

**Step 1.** Let O be the common centre, and let R and r be the radii of the greater and lesser spheres, respectively, so that R > r > 0 (D11.14, D11.16). Construct the mean proportional s between R and r; thus s² = Rr and r < s < R (6.13, 6.17; CN5). The natural preceding construction is 12.16: we shall use the same polygon both around an axis and in meridian sections. The mean proportional supplies the margin needed for these two directions. Products below denote rectangles, and squares denote squares on the indicated lengths.

**Step 2.** In a plane E through O, describe concentric circles of radii R and s (P3). By 12.16, inscribe in the greater circle an equilateral polygon G having an even number 2m of sides, with its sides wholly outside the lesser circle. Equal chords give equal successive arcs and equal central angles; consequently G is regular, and opposite vertices are endpoints of diameters (3.28, 3.27). Its sides have one common perpendicular distance a from O (1.12, 3.14). Therefore a > s. A perpendicular from O bisects its side, so the right triangle formed with a vertex gives a < R (3.3, 1.47; CN5). Write k = a/R; thus 0 < k < 1.

**Step 3.** Erect through O the diameter NS perpendicular to E (11.12), and label the vertices of G consecutively V₀, …, V₂ₘ₋₁. In each meridian half-plane bounded by NS and containing OVⱼ, copy the half of G running between two opposite vertices, placing those vertices at N and S. This is done by copying its central angles (1.23). Denote its successive vertices by A₀,ⱼ = N, A₁,ⱼ, …, Aₘ,ⱼ = S. These are finitely many positions of the same polygonal semicircle during the rotation defining the greater sphere; hence every Aᵢ,ⱼ lies on that sphere (D11.14; CN4).

For each fixed i, the corresponding vertices have the same height on NS and the same distance ρᵢ from it. If Hᵢ is their common perpendicular foot on NS, they therefore form a regular polygon in the plane through Hᵢ perpendicular to NS, with centre Hᵢ and circumradius ρᵢ. These assertions follow directly from the congruent meridian positions and their perpendiculars (1.12; D11.14; CN4). At i = 0 and i = m the polygon reduces to a pole.

**Step 4.** Fix adjacent meridians, indexed j and j + 1, taking indices cyclically. Let M be the midpoint of VⱼVⱼ₊₁, and let B be the plane through NS and OM (3.3, 11.2). For each nondegenerate ring, let Uᵢ be the midpoint of Aᵢ,ⱼAᵢ,ⱼ₊₁. The corresponding midpoint radius HᵢUᵢ lies in B and is perpendicular to that ring edge (3.3). The right triangles HᵢUᵢAᵢ,ⱼ and OMVⱼ are similar, since the rings have the same central angles. Hence
HᵢUᵢ / ρᵢ = OM / OVⱼ = a/R = k
(6.4). At a pole put Uᵢ equal to that pole; the equality HᵢUᵢ = kρᵢ then still holds.

**Step 5.** Each nondegenerate ring edge Aᵢ,ⱼAᵢ,ⱼ₊₁ is perpendicular to B. Indeed, it is perpendicular to HᵢUᵢ, and also to the line through Uᵢ parallel to NS: this latter line is perpendicular to the ring plane (1.31, 11.8; D11.3). These two intersecting lines lie in B, so 11.4 applies. Two consecutive ring edges are therefore parallel (11.6), and hence coplanar (D1.23). Joining corresponding endpoints produces a plane trapezium; at either pole it produces a plane triangle (P1, 11.2). Perform these joins for every pair of consecutive rings and every pair of adjacent meridians.

**Step 6.** The resulting trapezia and polar triangles form a closed polyhedral surface. Indeed, between consecutive ring planes, every section parallel to E is a regular polygon with corresponding vertices on the meridian edges; this follows from parallel-line proportions (6.2). These sections occur successively from N to S, and their interiors contain the intervening part of the axis. Thus the faces bound a solid K, and O is in its interior (D11.1, D11.2).

Moreover, K is inscribed in the greater sphere. All its vertices lie on that sphere by Step 3. A segment joining two points of the sphere lies inside it, by applying 3.2 in the plane through those points and O (11.2; D11.14). The same holds for two points already inside, by extending their line to the sphere (P2, 3.2). The filled ring polygons and the filled layers between them consist of such segments. Consequently the whole solid lies within the greater sphere.

**Step 7.** Consider any face between the two meridians fixed in Step 4, and let P be any point of that face. Its perpendicular projection onto B is a point Q of the segment UᵢUᵢ₊₁. To see this directly, draw through P the line parallel to the ring edges (1.31). Parallel-line proportions show that the midpoint of this section of the trapezium or triangle lies on UᵢUᵢ₊₁; for a parallelogram the same assertion follows from its equal opposite sides (6.2, 1.34). That line is perpendicular to B, since it is parallel to a line perpendicular to B (11.8). Its midpoint is therefore Q. If P already lies in B, take Q = P. Since O lies in B,
OP² = OQ² + PQ²,
and consequently OP ≥ OQ (D11.3, 1.47).

**Step 8.** In B, copy the original polygonal semicircle from N to S, on the side containing the Uᵢ, and call its corresponding vertices Cᵢ (1.23; CN4). Thus Cᵢ has foot Hᵢ on NS and HᵢCᵢ = ρᵢ. By Step 4,
HᵢUᵢ = k·HᵢCᵢ.
Accordingly, UᵢUᵢ₊₁ is obtained from CᵢCᵢ₊₁ by reducing all distances perpendicular to NS in the fixed ratio k, while preserving their heights.

More explicitly, for every Q on UᵢUᵢ₊₁ there is a point Y on CᵢCᵢ₊₁ with the same perpendicular foot T on NS and with TQ = k·TY. If the original side meets NS when produced, this follows by applying the intercept theorem and similar triangles with that intersection as vertex (6.2, 6.4). If the side is parallel to NS, it follows from the equal opposite sides of the resulting parallelograms (1.34).

**Step 9.** The side CᵢCᵢ₊₁ has perpendicular distance a from O, because it belongs to a congruent copy of G (3.14; CN4). Dropping the perpendicular from O to that side and applying 1.47 gives OY² ≥ a² (1.12, 1.47). Applying 1.47 also to the perpendiculars at T, and using 0 < k < 1, gives
OQ² = OT² + TQ²
= OT² + k²TY²
≥ k²OT² + k²TY²
= k²OY²
≥ k²a².
Here the inequality follows by comparing a square with the smaller similar square (CN5). Hence, together with Step 7, OP ≥ OQ ≥ ka.

**Step 10.** Since a > s and s² = Rr,
ka = a²/R > s²/R = r.
The strict comparison follows by comparing the squares and then rectangles of the same altitude R (6.17, 6.1; CN5). Thus every point P on every face of K satisfies OP > r, including all edges and vertices.

Since O is inside K, no radius of the lesser sphere can leave K: its first exit would be a boundary point at distance at most r, contradicting the inequality just proved (D11.2). Therefore the lesser sphere lies strictly inside K, and no part of the surface of K touches it. The solid K is the required polyhedral solid inscribed in the greater sphere.
